quoted_clause: The KV moves once per request, then stays local (ownership splits); the split itself exists because the two stages want opposite resources under load — prefill needs compute capacity (per-request ~1.19 PFLOPS over the ~1.08 s prefill budget vs 0.989 peak single-H100; on the canonical 8×H100 host the same prefill takes ~0.47 s at 35% MFU, Ch 12), while decode needs HBM bandwidth (at batch size 1 and 25 ms TPOT — 40 tokens/s — the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU, sharded to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU under the canonical 8×H100 host, Ch 6; batching divides the rate proportionally) [1P][DERIVED].
observed: The figure caption contains approximately 100 words of dense numerical derivation (prefill FLOP budget, MFU, weight-read rate, per-GPU sharding) that duplicates content already present in the body text of §3 'When to Disaggregate'. A reader encountering the figure receives a wall of numbers before processing the visual.
evidence: The same derivations (1.19 PFLOPS / 1.08 s / 0.989 peak / 0.47 s at 35% MFU / 5.6 TB/s / 3.35 TB/s / 0.70 TB/s) appear in both the body paragraph and the caption. The caption's primary job — telling the reader what to learn from the figure — is buried under derivation content that belongs in body text or Note 11.3-1.
root_cause: The caption was used as a location for the full derivation rather than a pointer to the body text's derivation.
correction: Shorten the caption to state the figure's key insight (e.g., 'The KV moves once per request, then stays local; the split exists because prefill needs compute capacity while decode needs HBM bandwidth — see §3 and Note 11.3-1 for the derivations.') and move any unique numerical content not already in the body into Note 11.3-1 or the body text.
acceptance_test: The caption is under ~40 words, states what the reader should learn from the figure, and does not duplicate numerical derivations already present in the body text.

page_hint: §6, 'What the capability table does not promise'
quoted_clause: ### What the capability table does not promise
observed: This section (~500 words) covers two distinct topics without clear internal separation: (a) qualifying the capability table (quantization support ≠ end-to-end support, deployment record requirements) and (b) introducing serving qualification for diverse model classes (diffusion language models, adaptive depth, early exit, seven-gate record). The transition from (a) to (b) occurs at 'A serving feature belongs to an algorithm path' but is not marked by a subheading or explicit signpost, so the reader may lose track of the section's original purpose (qualifying Table 11-2).
evidence: The section opens by referencing the capability table, then pivots to diffusion schedulers, refinement rounds, FDFO scheduling, adaptive depth, depth distributions, and economic denominators — topics that go well beyond qualifying a table. The seven-gate qualification record at the end is a standalone framework that could serve as its own subsection.
root_cause: Two related but distinct pedagogical goals (table qualification and model-class qualification) were merged into one section without structural markers.
correction: Add an intermediate subheading (e.g., '#### Serving qualification for diverse model classes') at the pivot point 'A serving feature belongs to an algorithm path', or split into two subsections: one for table qualification and one for model-class qualification with the seven-gate record as a concluding framework.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify the section's two main topics from the headings alone, and the transition between them is explicitly marked.

quoted_clause: under the canonical 8xH100 TP=8 host
observed: Uses lowercase 'x' in '8xH100' while the same paragraph and the rest of the chapter use the multiplication sign '×' in '8×H100' (e.g., 'under the canonical 8×H100 host', 'on the canonical 8×H100 host', 'one 8×H100 replica').
evidence: Direct comparison of the two spellings within §3 and across the chapter.
root_cause: Typographic inconsistency during editing.
correction: Change '8xH100' to '8×H100' for consistency with the rest of the chapter.
acceptance_test: A case-insensitive search for '8xH100' in Chapter 11 returns zero results; all instances use '8×H100'.

quoted_clause: at the replica's admitted load (≈1.3-2 req/s per Ch 14 Step 3)
observed: Uses a hyphen '-' for the numeric range '1.3-2' while §3 uses an en-dash '–' for the same range: 'per-host ≈1.3–2 req/s'.
evidence: Direct comparison of the two range notations in §3 and §6.
root_cause: Typographic inconsistency; hyphen used where en-dash is the correct range separator.
correction: Change '≈1.3-2 req/s' to '≈1.3–2 req/s' in §6 to match §3 and standard range typography.
acceptance_test: All numeric ranges in Chapter 11 use en-dash (–), not hyphen (-).

quoted_clause: The batch is locked until its *slowest* member finishes (fits-all-in-one-run)
observed: The parenthetical '(fits-all-in-one-run)' is awkward compound-adjective phrasing that is not standard terminology and could confuse readers. It appears to mean 'all requests fit in one run/batch' but the hyphenation makes it read as a single compound modifier.
evidence: The phrase does not appear elsewhere in the chapter and is not defined. Standard terminology for this behavior is 'run-to-completion' or simply 'the batch runs to completion'.
root_cause: Non-standard coinage used as a parenthetical gloss.
correction: Replace with a standard phrase: '(the batch runs to completion)' or simply remove the parenthetical, since the preceding clause 'locked until its slowest member finishes' already conveys the meaning.
acceptance_test: The parenthetical is either removed or replaced with a standard, self-explanatory phrase.

quoted_clause: idle bubbles at the end of every batch
observed: The phrase 'idle bubbles' could be misread as GPU idleness, but in context it refers to batch-slot idleness (finished requests leave empty slots while the longest request continues). The GPU is still doing work — just with a reduced effective batch size. The next bullet ('the GPU drains (no work) then floods') correctly describes actual GPU idleness between batches, creating a potential confusion between the two types of idleness.
evidence: In discrete batching, when short outputs finish, their slots become empty but the GPU continues processing the longest request. The GPU is not idle; the batch is underutilized. The phrase 'idle bubbles at the end of every batch' is ambiguous between slot-level and GPU-level idleness.
root_cause: Imprecise wording that conflates slot idleness with GPU idleness.
correction: Clarify: 'empty trailing slots reduce the effective batch size while the longest request finishes' or 'the batch shrinks as short outputs complete, reducing utilization'.
acceptance_test: The sentence unambiguously describes slot-level underutilization (not GPU idleness) during the trailing phase of a batch.

quoted_clause: The four are independent dials — mechanisms can be combined in principle, subject to implementation support and resource interactions
observed: The word 'independent' in 'independent dials' suggests the four mechanisms do not affect each other, but the immediately following clause acknowledges 'resource interactions' (e.g., prefix caching and continuous batching drawing on the same KV pool). The figure title uses 'separable concerns, not a stack' — 'separable' is the more accurate term (addressable in any order) while 'independent' overstates the claim.
evidence: The figure title says 'separable' and the description says 'independent'; these are different claims. Separable = can be addressed in any order. Independent = do not affect each other. The text's own parenthetical example (shared KV pool) demonstrates they are not independent.
root_cause: Word choice drift between figure title ('separable') and figure description ('independent').
correction: Change 'independent dials' to 'separable dials' or 'independently addressable dials' to match the figure title and the acknowledged resource interactions.
acceptance_test: The figure description uses 'separable' or an equivalent term consistent with the figure title and the acknowledged interactions.

quoted_clause: Bigger discrete batches raise raw tokens/s but push TTFT past the SLO, zeroing goodput (Ch6).
observed: 'Zeroing goodput' reads as 'goodput becomes zero' (all requests miss the SLO), which is stronger than the evidence supports. In practice, larger batches increase average TTFT and cause more requests to miss the SLO, reducing goodput — but not necessarily reducing it to zero. Some requests may still meet the SLO.
evidence: Goodput is defined as tokens/s arriving before the SLO deadline (§4). Larger batches push the TTFT distribution rightward; requests in the left tail may still meet the 2 s p95 SLO. 'Zeroing' implies the entire goodput contribution is eliminated.
root_cause: Hyperbolic phrasing in a common-mistakes bullet that overstates the consequence.
correction: Replace 'zeroing goodput' with 'collapsing goodput' or 'driving goodput toward zero as more requests miss the SLO deadline'.
acceptance_test: The corrected phrasing does not imply goodput reaches exactly zero, while still conveying that goodput degrades severely.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (worked example) and Ch 13 §3 (placing the canonical workload); also Table 12-1 footnote
quoted_clause: The KV cache for 9.2K context at FP16 precision ... approximately 24 GB ... [Ch 13] KV for the 9.5K max context at FP16 ≈ 24.9 GB; inference residency ≈ 165 GB
observed: Ch 12 computes KV at 9.2K context (input only) giving ~24 GB and total residency 164 GB. Ch 13 computes KV at 9.5K context (input + output) giving ~24.9 GB and total residency ~165 GB. The capacity screen used throughout (17.5 requests/host = floor(436/24.9)) is based on the 9.5K figure. Table 12-1 notes the numerical difference ('Ch 13's 9.5K basis gives ~165 GB') but never explains WHY the bases differ. A reader deriving 17.5 from Ch 12's 24 GB figure gets 436/24 = 18.2, not 17.5.
evidence: 436/24 = 18.17 vs 436/24.9 = 17.51. The 17-slot floor used in all host-count arithmetic (Ch 12 §3, Ch 13 §3, Ch 13 §8) comes from the 9.5K basis, but Ch 12's worked example only establishes the 9.2K basis.
root_cause: Two different context-length bases (input-only 9.2K vs input+output 9.5K) are used for KV sizing across chapters without a conceptual explanation of when each is appropriate. The Table 12-1 footnote flags the number but not the reason.
correction: Add one sentence in Ch 12 §3 or §4 explaining that prefill-time KV covers the 9.2K input while maximum per-request KV (used for concurrency/capacity screens) covers 9.5K (input + output), and that the 17-slot figure derives from the 9.5K basis. Alternatively, use 9.5K consistently in Ch 12's worked example and note that prefill-time KV is slightly smaller.
acceptance_test: A reader can derive 17.5 slots/host from numbers presented in Ch 12 alone, or Ch 12 explicitly states which basis the 17-slot figure uses and why.

quoted_clause: the gate closes only when the host class is replicated to ~5 hosts on the average prefill screen (92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65 → 5), ~6 on the average KV/service-time screen (10 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 5.06 → 6), and ~21 at peak (40 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 20.2 → 21) (Chs. 15–17)
observed: The numbers 17 (KV slots per host) and 8.6 s (service time) are used in Ch 12's host-count arithmetic without being derived or restated in Ch 12. The cross-reference '(Chs. 15–17)' points forward, not to where these numbers are established. The reader encountering Ch 12 cannot verify these calculations without external chapters.
evidence: 17 = floor(436/24.9) = floor(17.51); 8.6 s is referenced as 'canonical' but its derivation is not in this chapter. Ch 12 derives 436 GB ('640 − 140 weights − ~64 runtime ≈ 436 GB, Ch 7/17') but stops there.
root_cause: Key inputs to the host-count formula are established in earlier chapters but not restated or briefly derived where they are first used in arithmetic.
correction: Add a parenthetical in Ch 12 §3 at the first use: e.g., '(17 = floor of the 436 GB KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per-request KV at 9.5K; 8.6 s = the canonical service time from Ch 7)'. This costs one line and makes the arithmetic self-contained.
acceptance_test: A reader can follow the host-count arithmetic in Ch 12 §3 without leaving the chapter to look up 17 or 8.6.

page_hint: Ch 13 §2 (Mental Model), bullet list under 'classic triggers for climbing'
quoted_clause: Latency/geography: SLO can't be met due to distance or contention → split prefill/decode (a within-tier move).
observed: This bullet is listed under 'The classic triggers for climbing' but its stated response ('split prefill/decode') is explicitly labeled 'a within-tier move' — i.e., NOT a climb. The first three bullets all describe responses that involve climbing to a higher tier; this one does not. The structure implies trigger → climb, but this bullet breaks that pattern without explanation.
evidence: Bullets 1–3: Memory → cluster (climb); KV residency → single host (climb from Local to Server); Traffic → cluster (climb). Bullet 4: Latency/geography → within-tier move (no climb). The section header says 'triggers for climbing'.
root_cause: The bullet conflates a trigger (latency/geography problem) with a response that happens to be within-tier, placed in a list whose other entries all produce tier escalation.
correction: Either (a) move this bullet out of the 'triggers for climbing' list into a separate note about within-tier responses to latency problems, or (b) restructure it to show that latency/geography can trigger either a within-tier response (P/D disaggregation) or a placement response (moving closer, which is de-escalation), making clear which is a climb and which is not.
acceptance_test: Every bullet under 'triggers for climbing' describes a response that actually climbs a tier, or the section explicitly notes which bullets describe within-tier responses.

quoted_clause: KV residency per GPU: model + KV no longer fits one GPU → single host — the within-tier step Fig 13.1 shows between Single GPU and Single host.
observed: Single GPU = Local/edge tier; Single host = Server tier (per the Fig 13.1 caption: 'Single GPU = Local/edge, Single host = Server'). These are DIFFERENT tiers. Calling the step between them 'within-tier' is incorrect or at minimum deeply confusing.
evidence: Fig 13.1 caption explicitly maps: Single GPU = Local/edge, Single host = Server, Multi-host = Cluster, Cluster/fleet = Hyperscale fleet. The step from Single GPU to Single host crosses the Local/edge → Server boundary.
root_cause: The term 'within-tier' is used where 'inter-tier' or 'up one rung' is meant, or the author considers Local/edge and Server to be 'within' the same broad category — but the chapter's own tier definitions say otherwise.
correction: Replace 'within-tier step' with 'one-rung step' or 'inter-tier step (Local/edge → Server)' to match the chapter's own tier definitions.
acceptance_test: The terminology for the Single GPU → Single host transition is consistent with the four-tier definitions in §13.1 and the Fig 13.1 caption.

quoted_clause: a bounded set of two to three candidates, each designed to probe a distinct gate — memory fit, throughput, or quality
observed: The claim says each candidate probes a distinct gate from the set {memory fit, throughput, quality}. The actual candidates: (a) open gate = throughput; (b) open gate = throughput at single prefill host; (c) open gate = quality. No candidate has memory fit as its open gate. (a) and (b) probe the same gate (throughput). The claim of three distinct gates probed by three candidates is not realized.
evidence: Open-gate table in Ch 12: (a) throughput open; (b) throughput open at a single prefill host; (c) quality open. Memory fit passes for all three candidates (164 < 640, 164 < 640, 15 < 80).
root_cause: The opening paragraph promises a one-to-one mapping between candidates and gates, but the worked example produces two throughput-probing candidates and one quality-probing candidate, with memory fit never binding.
correction: Either (a) revise the claim to 'each designed to probe a different aspect of the constraint set — single-host throughput, phase-split throughput, or quality-vs-size' or (b) add a fourth candidate where memory fit is the binding constraint (e.g., a model that barely fits one host, forcing a memory-driven design choice), or (c) soften to 'each designed to stress-test the gates from a different angle'.
acceptance_test: The opening claim about distinct gates matches the actual open-gate distribution of the candidates presented in §12.3.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (candidate a description) vs Table 12-1 vs unnumbered open-gate table
quoted_clause: conditional finalist [Table 12-1] vs Candidates (a) and (b) carry forward as finalists [§12.6] vs the finalists are Candidates (a) and (b) [§12.8]
observed: Table 12-1 labels (a) and (b) as 'conditional finalist'. §12.6 and §12.8 call them 'finalists' without the 'conditional' qualifier. The word 'conditional' implies they haven't fully passed yet, while 'finalist' implies they have.
evidence: Table 12-1 verdict column: 'conditional finalist' for both (a) and (b). §12.6: 'Candidates (a) and (b) carry forward as finalists'. §12.8: 'the finalists are Candidates (a) and (b)'.
root_cause: Terminology drift between the table and the prose.
correction: Use 'conditional finalist' consistently in prose, or drop 'conditional' from the table. The mini-case's phrasing ('the finalists are Candidates (a) and (b)') is acceptable if 'finalist' is defined as 'advanced to evaluation' rather than 'passed all gates'.
acceptance_test: The same term is used for the same status in Table 12-1, §12.6, and §12.8.

quoted_clause: Economics is therefore recorded as *not yet passed (deferred)*
observed: §12.1 explicitly states 'The economic ceiling is recorded but is not one of the three gates'. The mini-case then says economics is 'not yet passed (deferred)'. 'Not yet passed' implies economics IS a gate that will be evaluated later, contradicting 'not one of the three gates'. 'Deferred' is consistent with 'recorded but not a gate'.
evidence: §12.1: 'The economic ceiling is recorded but is not one of the three gates; §12.8 states its consequence at fleet scale.' §12.8: 'Economics is therefore recorded as *not yet passed (deferred)*'.
root_cause: The phrase 'not yet passed' uses gate language for something the chapter explicitly says is not a gate.
correction: Replace with 'Economics is therefore recorded as failing at fleet scale (deferred to Ch 16 for resolution)' or 'Economics is recorded as not met at fleet scale; it is not one of the three gates but its consequence is material.'
acceptance_test: The mini-case's economics wording does not use gate-passing language for something §12.1 says is not a gate.

page_hint: Ch 13 §3 (Escalating: When 10× Traffic Forces the Cluster Tier)
quoted_clause: At ~100 rps × 9.5K tokens = ~950K tokens/s, one host's goodput is exceeded.
observed: The 950K figure uses total tokens per request (9.5K = 9.2K input + 300 output), but the subsequent host-count calculation uses the KV/service-time screen (based on 8.6 s service time and 17 slots), not a total-tokens/s comparison. The prefill screen elsewhere uses 9.2K input tokens (920K input tokens/s at 100 rps). The 950K figure is not used in any calculation and mixes total-token demand with a discussion of prefill capacity.
evidence: 100 × 9,500 = 950,000 (total tokens). 100 × 9,200 = 920,000 (input tokens). The host count uses ⌈100 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = 51, which is a KV/service-time screen, not a tokens/s screen. The 950K number appears only as an illustrative magnitude.
root_cause: The text uses total tokens to establish that one host is insufficient, but the metric doesn't match the screen that follows, and the number isn't used downstream.
correction: Either use input tokens consistently ('~920K input tokens/s, far above one host's ~19.8K prefill ceiling') or explicitly note that 950K is total-token demand shown for magnitude while the host count uses the KV/service-time screen.
acceptance_test: The token-demand figure in the escalation paragraph matches the metric used in the subsequent host-count calculation, or the mismatch is explicitly noted.

quoted_clause: continuous batching on 8×H100 at ~9.5K tokens/request sustained roughly tens of thousands of tokens/s
observed: 'Tens of thousands of tokens/s' is vague and does not specify whether this refers to prefill tokens/s (~19.8K), decode tokens/s, or total tokens/s. The surrounding context discusses prefill capacity, but the phrase could be read as total throughput.
evidence: Ch 12 establishes ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s for the 70B on 8×H100. The phrase 'tens of thousands' is consistent with this but doesn't specify the metric.
root_cause: Deliberate vagueness in a conceptual discussion, but the vagueness obscures which resource is being discussed.
correction: Replace with 'sustained roughly ~20K prefill-tokens/s (Ch 8)' or 'roughly tens of thousands of prefill-tokens/s' to specify the metric.
acceptance_test: The throughput figure in the escalation paragraph specifies prefill vs decode vs total.

quoted_clause: 24,725 exact: 989 TFLOP/s × 35% MFU ÷ 14 GFLOP/token
observed: The word 'exact' is used for 24,725, but the inputs are approximate: 989 TFLOPS is a vendor spec (dense FP16), 35% MFU is an assumption, and 14 GFLOP/token is a first-order approximation (2 × 7B, ignoring attention quadratic term and other details). The calculation is exact GIVEN the inputs, but the inputs are not exact.
evidence: 989 × 10^12 × 0.35 / (14 × 10^9) = 24,725. But 14 GFLOP/token for a 7B model is approximate (actual depends on architecture, attention heads, etc.), and 35% MFU is an assumption.
root_cause: 'Exact' conflates arithmetic precision with input precision.
correction: Replace 'exact' with '24,725 (from the stated inputs)' or '~24,725' to match the tilde used for the comparable 70B figure (~2,472).
acceptance_test: Numbers derived from approximate inputs are not labeled 'exact'.

page_hint: Ch 12 Table 12-2 (Monthly fully loaded cost row) and §12.8
observed: The figure $155,816.93 is presented with two decimal places, suggesting cent-level precision. The inputs (host cost, energy, utilization) are approximate. The per-1K figure uses ≈ but the total does not.
evidence: $155,816.93 / 6,240 = $24.9707... ≈ $24.97. The total is presented as exact while the derived per-1K uses ≈.
root_cause: False precision: the total inherits precision from a calculation in Ch 16 but the inputs are estimates.
correction: Either present the total as ~$155.8K (matching the ≈ used elsewhere) or add a note that the figure is the output of Ch 16's cost model and its precision reflects the model's arithmetic, not measurement accuracy.
acceptance_test: Cost figures use consistent precision marking (either all exact-from-model or all approximate).

quoted_clause: with the KV hidden-state handed between them (Splitwise / DistServe / Mooncake)
observed: Three named systems (Splitwise, DistServe, Mooncake) are cited without bibliographic references. For a technical handbook, named systems should have citations.
evidence: No citation markers or reference entries accompany these names in the chunk.
root_cause: Named systems used as evidence without source attribution.
correction: Add citation markers (e.g., [S1], [S2], [S3]) and corresponding entries in the reference list, or add a footnote with paper titles and years.
acceptance_test: Every named system used as evidence has a resolvable citation.
